channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Arreola Histórica, the digital repository of the Juan José Arreola Public Library, is inaugurated.
item.description: From the University of Guadalajara and machine-translated from Spanish: “It seeks to streamline access to the more than 200,000 files that have already been digitized, a systematic effort spanning more than 20 years. A new access point to the digital archive of the Juan José Arreola State Public Library of Jalisco (BPEJ) is now available: Arreola Histórica . This repository, accessible to anyone with internet access, contains over 200,000 digitized items, and it is estimated that the total collection comprises between 4 and 5 million items.”

item.title: The Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum Press Office Background Briefings Opened and Digitized
item.description: Richard Nixon Presidential Library: “The Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum has made available to the public the newly opened and digitized Background Briefings series, part of the White House Central Files: Staff Member and Office Files: White House Press Office collection.”

item.title: Yearbooks Now Available Online Through ScholarHub@UA Little Rock
item.description: University of Arkansas Little Rock: “As UA Little Rock celebrates its Centennial Year, Ottenheimer Library is helping preserve the stories that have shaped the university’s history. Yearbooks dating from 1931 to 1973 have been digitized and are now available online through ScholarHub@UA Little Rock, the university’s Institutional Repository.”

item.title: My To Do – Replacing what Microsoft is Killing
item.description: Raymond Camden: “Earlier this week I shared the bad news that Microsoft is killing off To Do, one of the best, simplest apps around. I built a simple export tool to let you get your existing To Dos in either JSON or HTML format. At the time, I hinted at a plan to replace the app, and today I’m happy to share it.”

item.title: Arm strongarms site that hosts ad-free documentation and it may disappear
item.description: The Register: “The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as ‘without a million popups and all of the bloat’ that Arm provides on its own. According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.”

item.title: Australia passes online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines
item.description: Associated Press: “Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.”

item.title: Balint introduces bill on data privacy protections, tech guidelines for schools
item.description: VT Digger: “U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt, introduced a bill Tuesday designed to ensure big tech companies protect personal student data. The bill would require tech companies that provide services to schools and other educational institutions to keep identifiable student information private.”

item.title: ‘Wifi Motion Sensing’ Can Track Everything You Do Through Your Router
item.description: Lifehacker: “While the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home users might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks. So here’s how wifi routers sense motion, what they can do with it, who has access to the data, and how you can disable it.”

item.title: Azerbaijan, Vatican expand cooperation on digital preservation of historical heritage [PHOTOS]
item.description: Azernews: “A new agreement on the study and implementation of digital preservation techniques at the Vatican Apostolic Archive has been signed, building on the Memorandum of Understanding concluded between the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and the Vatican Apostolic Library and Archive in 2025.”

item.title: Nearly 400,000 spectators take in light show at Swiss parliament
item.description: SwissInfo: “Over 36 evenings and a total of 108 performances, this year’s festival offered a glimpse into Swiss wildlife through the changing seasons. Marshes teeming with herons and frogs, an autumnal forest where squirrels frolic, snow-covered mountain landscapes, and colourful scenes featuring fluttering butterflies were projected onto the facades of the parliament building.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: HHS Launches ‘Radical Transparency’ Website, Makes Tens of Thousands of Government Records Accessible to Americans
item.description: US Department of Health and Human Services: “The website replaces HHS’ ‘Online Reading Room,’ bringing records previously released under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and other public agency documents into one searchable location. Featured records include a newly released Biden-era NIH memo examining whether the agency should leave Twitter after Elon Musk’s acquisition, along with Secretary Kennedy’s calendars. HHS will add records as they become publicly available.”

item.title: Dev Material Archive
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: “This is an archive of written articles about web development, web design, and web accessibility that once existed on the World Wide Web and which would otherwise be lost to time. Publications close, SEO strategies change, rights lapse, standards alter, content management systems are migrated between, acquisitions happen, websites get redesigned.”

item.title: The Ladybird Browser Reaches Alpha
item.description: Hackaday: “If we learned one thing form the browser wars of the 2000s, it’s that having a single ecosystem dominate the internet is best avoided. Yet here we are in 2026, and through Google’s Blink and Apple’s Webkit, we have very little diversity in the world of web browsing engines. Firefox is now very much an outsider, and that’s pretty much it. But there is another up-and-coming fully-featured browser, Ladybird, and it’s now available in alpha form for those of you with macOS or Linux.”

item.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 writer leaves social media following online harassment
item.description: Video Games Chronicle: “Alexa D’Agostino, who also has thank-you credits on GTA 5, Red Dead Online, and GTA: Online, has been targeted by people online who dislike the inclusion of Lucia in GTA 6. D’Agostino had previously spoken about some of the writing inspirations behind her work on Lucia. A thread on X detailing why these people are targeting D’Agostino cites her support of LGBTQ+ pride and posts that are critical of US President Donald Trump.”

item.title: New Zealand Fashion Museum Launches An Urgent Appeal To Keep New Zealand’s Fashion Story Alive And Online
item.description: New Zealand Fashion Museum: “New Zealand Fashion Museum (NZFM) has enough money in the bank to continue operating for two to three months before it must let go of its only paid part-time contractor. Today it launches an urgent GiveALittle appeal to raise $25,000, a year’s running costs…”

item.title: Baltimore and the Ravens rally around The Poe House, raising $100,000 for its preservation
item.description: The Baltimore Banner: “This summer, things were looking bleak for the Edgar Allan Poe House and Museum. The demolition of dilapidated public housing was rattling the little two-story brick home built in 1830, and it also had experienced break-ins and vandalism. The museum put out a call for help to preserve the historic site, and Baltimoreans responded. The nonprofit that runs the museum sent a fundraising goal of $50,000; it has raised more than twice that amount, including a $50,000 donation from the Ravens.”

item.title: Amazon Must Face $1.7 Billion Lawsuit Over Alleged Collection of Facial Data Through Its Photos Service
item.description: PetaPixel: “Amazon must face a class-action lawsuit on behalf of potentially hundreds of thousands of Amazon Photos users over allegations that it collected facial biometric data from their photographs without their consent.”

item.title: Bill Would Put All Broadband Grant Programs Into Database
item.description: Law360: “Senator Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, and Reps. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., and August Pfluger, R-Texas, have introduced the PROTOCOL Act, which, if passed, would mandate the creation of a single database where all federal broadband funding can be looked up. This will prevent companies interested in participating in broadband programs from having to check in on the requirements for 133 individual programs, the lawmakers said.”

item.title: Following a stranger on Instagram for three days may reduce prejudice, a study finds
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Two of the fictional Instagram profiles had German-sounding names while the other two had Arabic- or Turkish- sounding names. Each participant followed one of them for three days and saw ordinary, everyday posts like parks and building facades. Afterwards, participants rated people from Turkish or Arab backgrounds in Germany as warmer and more competent.”

item.title: I Created a Completely Fresh Instagram Account, Searched for Some Innocuous Terms Related to Judaism, and My Feed Almost Instantly Became a Cesspool of Overt Nazism
item.description: Futurism: “This geyser of overt Nazism and bigotry is on a brand-new Instagram account I’d registered the day prior. Since creating it, I hadn’t liked or shared any posts, nor followed any accounts. Instead, all I did was search for a few neutral terms related to Judaism — and Meta’s algorithm did the rest, transforming my feed into a bottomless pit of hate speech and misinformation.”

item.title: How little free libraries are making a difference in Colorado’s book deserts
item.description: Colorado Sun: “Huerfano County, southwest of Pueblo, is considered a ‘book desert,’ a term coined in 2014 by the Fort Collins publishing company Unite for Literacy. The publisher worked with Colorado State University researchers to map out the likelihood that a house has 100 or more books. Their model considered variables like access to early childhood education centers, adult education levels and economic status to predict whether a house was likely to hit the 100 book threshold, which has been linked to better academic outcomes.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: UHI to launch multilingual Island Voices archive with Inverness film night
item.description: University of the Highlands and Islands: “The archive preserves the first 21 years of Island Voices/Guthan nan Eilean, a community project founded by Gordon Wells in 2005. Rooted in Gaelic-speaking communities, it captures ‘slices of life in and beyond the 21st century Hebrides’, with people sharing their stories, knowledge and experiences in their own words. Visitors can explore conversations, memories, songs, poetry and documentaries in languages including Gaelic, English, Scots, Shaetlan, Irish and Welsh. International collaborations extend to South Asia and the Caribbean.”

item.title: Tinos Launches Digital Platform to Protect its Iconic Dovecotes
item.description: Tovima: “As part of ongoing efforts to preserve its unique architectural heritage, the Greek island of Tinos announced this week the launch of its first digital platform dedicated to documenting and safeguarding its famous dovecotes.”

item.title: Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta)
item.description: Kagi Blog: “We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time – the public beta of Kagi Mail. A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains.”

item.title: Proton Drive can now move your files out of Google Drive with one click
item.description: TechSpot: “Proton AG is adding more tools that let cloud users easily switch to one of the company’s secure services. Having already introduced email migration features, the Switzerland-based organization is now promoting an easy way to move data away from Google Drive.”

item.title: These New Yorkers ditched their smartphones for a month. No, seriously.
item.description: Gothamist: “Being phone-free for the night was a requirement for those who wanted to party with the roughly 100 New Yorkers who had just given up their smartphones for a month. Friends and families were invited to celebrate along with them — and see a showcase of hobbies and art projects that were picked up during the month instead of screens.”

item.title: Book and Reading Tracker Apps
item.description: Explicating Elle: “But the problem is, like with Twitter/X and all the clones that didn’t capture the original magic or the majority of the user base, there are lots of smaller Goodreads replacements, with a different focus or look, and nothing quite works like Goodreads used to. Here is a list of the apps I have tried.”

item.title: Tailgating Past Gates And Dodging Process Server: Judge Clears New Path To Serve Elon Musk In Defamation Suit
item.description: Tampa Free Press: “After months of dead-end addresses, unanswered phone calls, and a process server tailgating a car into a gated Texas neighborhood, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., has cleared a new path for a Maryland man trying to serve Elon Musk with a defamation lawsuit. …[Daniel Berulis] claims Musk posted his photo and full name on X alongside an accusation that Berulis had filed a false whistleblower claim.”

item.title: Dutch Watchdog Says Smart Glasses That Record People Are ‘Unsafe’
item.description: PetaPixel: “The Dutch Data Protection Authority has advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses, warning that the devices pose risks to both users and bystanders. The recommendation follows an investigation into six models available on the Dutch market, which identified problems involving privacy, safety, and software security.”

item.title: How I Fixed My LinkedIn Feed
item.description: Pawel Brodzinski: “The fundamental difference between the standard LinkedIn feed and my custom prototype is that the former aims for engagement (counted as screen time), while the latter revolves around human connection.”

item.title: Can It Run Doom? Apparently, So Can a 3D Printer
item.description: Hackernoon: “But now Doom can run on everything. Today, I will be adding to that collection with an Ender 3 3D printer and going through my experience and thought process doing so.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Moving Image Archive
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: From the About page: “The Moving Image Archive is a searchable library of archival films. The material is drawn from public-domain collections and is free to reuse.” The gallery lists 2280 films / 122,218 clips.

item.title: Azerbaijan launches digital archive honouring general Samad bey Mehmandarov
item.description: Azernews: “The Republican Youth Library named after Jafar Jabbarli has launched a digital database commemorating the 170th anniversary of Samad bey Mehmandarov, a prominent military commander who left an indelible mark on Azerbaijan’s military history. Mehmandarov served as Minister of War of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic and held the rank of full artillery general.”

item.title: Historic Estes Park newspapers digitized through 2012
item.description: Estes Park Trail-Gazette (Colorado): “Estes Park newspapers dating from 1908 through April 2012 are now available… Readers can browse and keyword-search full-color, page-by-page reproductions of the papers, including articles, photographs and advertisements.”

item.title: Join the WordPress 7.2 Release Celebration Livestream
item.description: WordPress: “On December 8, 2026, at 16:00 UTC, contributors to WordPress 7.2 will livestream the release, and you’re invited. Expect demos of what’s new and time to hear from the contributors themselves. Anyone can watch and ask questions.”

item.title: Napster, LimeWire, and Trillian are still alive, just not how you remember them
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I used Trillian all the time. It was the one window that held every chat network I used, and when those networks died off, I assumed Trillian went with them. It didn’t. Trillian is still around, and it’s far from the only 2000s staple that’s technically still alive under its original name. The only catch is that most of these programs aren’t what they were, with many pivoting into completely new focuses that don’t align with the old name at all.”

item.title: Fake and AI generated ICE raid photos are popping up across California. Here’s how to verify ICE sightings
item.description: Los Angeles Public Press: “Groups that patrol for ICE told LA Public Press verifying activity starts with being at the scene, if you feel safe doing so, and examining activity yourself. Online guides and in-person events train people how to safely identify agents. But verifying whether an image of ICE activity is AI is a new challenge emerging during the ongoing surge in California.”

item.title: A Wave of Data Leaks in Japan Comes From a Single Marketing Tool
item.description: Unseen Japan: “It’s been a rough two months for data security worldwide. Japan, in particular, has gotten hammered by attackers targeting a range of Japanese firms in a number of niches. The wave, coupled with recently discovered security vulnerabilities in a popular programming language, led several sites to restrict services out of an abundance of caution, much to the consternation of foreign Japanese culture fans. Things just got a lot worse.”

item.title: French chateau owner takes Google to court over fake reviews
item.description: The Connexion: “The owner of a chateau and guesthouse in the Burgundy region of France has taken Google to court over fake online reviews. Raoul Salama has been fighting for eight years to change the internet giant’s moderation practices, which allow false comments to impact business ratings. On October 12, Mr Salama attended the tribunal judiciaire de Chalon-sur-Saône to present his case at a hearing, with the verdict set to be delivered on January 12, 2027.”

item.title: Moral anger overrides credibility and accelerates the spread of misinformation online
item.description: PsyPost: “When people feel moral anger, they become more likely to share false information online and pay less attention to the credibility of the source. This emotional reaction lowers the cognitive threshold required to make a sharing decision, leading to faster and more impulsive social media habits. The findings were published in the journal Cognition and Emotion.”

item.title: SAA Statement on the Censorship of LGBTQ+ Archives Materials
item.description: Society of American Archivists: “When archivists create exhibits, websites, and other public-facing resources, they apply their expertise and specialized knowledge to produce the most fulsome, accurate, and engaging information possible. Interference in these efforts is censorship and is unacceptable in a pluralistic democracy built on the free exchange of ideas.”

item.title: Riot Games to fund restoration of rare Goryeo Buddhist painting
item.description: Korea Herald: “Riot Games is bringing a rare 14th-century Buddhist painting from the Goryeo Kingdom (918-1392) back to Korea from the United States for conservation, as the gaming giant continues its efforts to preserve and support Korean cultural heritage.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New Jersey puts liquor license records online
item.description: Jersey Vindicator: “New Jersey residents now have a way to find out who holds liquor licenses in their communities, where those licenses are located, and what types of alcohol sales they allow. The state has launched a searchable online dashboard that makes information about thousands of alcoholic beverage licenses available to the public, Attorney General Jennifer Davenport announced Oct. 18.”

item.title: Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026
item.description: Engadget: “The search giant has a tendency to shut down services when it feels they’re not serving its broader goals, and this has led to the discontinuation of products as diverse as Google Reader, Google+, Stadia, Google Glass, Google Hangouts and dozens of other utilities over the last 15 years. 2026 is no different, so let’s take a look at everything Google discontinued this year.”

item.title: Pakistan proposes SCO network, digital archive to protect cultural heritage
item.description: Daily Times (Pakistan): “Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Dr. Musadik Malik has proposed establishing an SCO-wide network of cultural institutions, a digital repository of shared heritage and a climate-resilient heritage framework to protect the region’s cultural legacy.”

item.title: Your “purchased” digital movies can disappear, here’s 5 times it’s already happened
item.description: How-To Geek: “When a digital store shows you a buy button, it used to be easy to believe you were getting something that’s yours for good. Unfortunately, ‘buy’ has become a completely misleading word for digital purchases. There are plenty of examples, and each one is a reminder that you don’t own anything you buy online.”

item.title: House Democrat investigates government agencies’ use of messaging apps to discuss official business
item.description: Spectrum News: “Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump’s administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.”

item.title: Woman admits to using Meta glasses to secretly record witnesses in federal drug trial
item.description: Action News 5: “An Alabama woman who was upset about the prosecution of a now-convicted drug ‘kingpin’admitted Thursday that she used special glasses to secretly record witnesses who testified at the trial in January. Tierra Shatalia ‘Badd Twin’ Douglas, 35, of Mobile, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness.”

item.title: Ethics and data journalism: adding a new dimension to the data journalism pyramid
item.description: Online Journalism Blog: “Here’s a version of the inverted pyramid of data journalism that shows ethical considerations at each stage, thanks to the research of Laurence Dierickx, Marilia Gehrke and Carl-Gustav Linden which I blogged about yesterday. The research maps the stages of the pyramid of data journalism to different categories and ethical justifications.”

item.title: Getting news on gaming platforms like Discord and Twitch is linked to more radical political views
item.description: PsyPost: “Young Europeans who get their news from gaming platforms like Discord, Steam, or Twitch tend to hold stronger radical political views than peers who rely on social media or traditional news, according to research published in Political Psychology.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Near East Relief Historical Society
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: a new digital archive from the “Between 1915 and 1930, ordinary Americans raised more than $116 million and provided food, shelter, medical care, and other assistance to over a million survivors and refugees of the Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian Genocides. The photographs, letters, records, and field reports preserved here document that relief effort and the experiences of the people it served.”

item.title: New Bike Index Tool Helps Consumers Figure Out Which E-Bikes Are Legal
item.description: StreetsBlog Cal: “Bike Index has launched a free E-Bike Rules Checker that lets riders, parents and shoppers look up a specific e-bike and see whether it’s legal in their state and who can ride it. No account is required.”

item.title: The Nest app is shutting down, and your saved clips won’t make the move
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Google announced on November 20 that the Nest app will shut down on January 25, 2027, on Android, iOS, TV, and the web at home.nest.com. To keep controlling Nest devices and getting notifications remotely, users will need the Google Home app, which requires a Google Account.”

item.title: Unveiling the All-New Firefox Add-on Developer Hub
item.description: Mozilla Blog: “Sixteen years ago, Mozilla launched the add-ons developer hub to be a one-stop shop for Firefox extension and theme creators. While it served our community well for a long time, we knew it was time for a modern upgrade. Today, we’re thrilled to announce a completely reimagined Firefox add-ons developer hub, rolling out this December.”

item.title: Afghan Women Turn To Social Media To Earn Living As Doors Close Offline
item.description: Radio Free Europe: “Afghan women who have had their lives sharply restricted by Taliban rule have responded by building personal brands on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube showing them cooking at home, shopping in bazaars, or meeting friends and family. Some film Kabul’s bustling shopping district, quiet backstreets, or new restaurants and cafes. Others focus on nature, and one has found a niche in poetry. For many, it has become a way to earn a living. For others, a personal space free from Taliban repression.”

item.title: Oregon and Virginia Sue SpaceX Over A.I.-Generated Sexualized Images
item.description: New York Times: “Oregon and Virginia on Monday sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, accusing the company of violating state consumer protection laws by providing an artificial intelligence tool that allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children.”

item.title: European Commission warns EU Academy users of data leak after AI-driven cyberattack
item.description: Associated Press: “The European Commission on Monday warned users of one of its websites that personal data has been leaked in a major AI-generated cyberattack that was launched on the EU institution last month. The European Union’s executive branch said the EU Academy website had been caught up in the cyberattack. The site offers courses and information about the 27-nation bloc’s policies to people outside EU institutions.”

item.title: Germany seems to be serious about a TikTok Europe takeover
item.description: Engadget: “The Donald Trump-backed plan that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok’s American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union. This week Germany and Austria proposed a similar move for the app’s European operation, and now the German government says that it has lined up investors willing to fork over as much as €25 billion (about $27.4 billion USD) to finance such an arrangement, Politico reports.”

item.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
item.description: ProPublica: “In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled ‘Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.’ The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.”

item.title: Utah historian seeks help finding remaining copies of first Japanese newspaper
item.description: KJZZ: “The Rocky Mountain Times was Utah’s first Japanese-language newspaper published and circulated during the early 1900s. So far, only one photograph has been found, giving further visual proof of the newspaper’s existence.”

item.title: The earlier kids join social media, the lower their test scores tend to be, study finds
item.description: PsyPost: “A study of high school students in Lombardy, a region in northern Italy, found that students who created a personal social media account in 6th, 7th, or 8th grade tended to score lower on standardized tests of Italian and mathematics than peers who waited until 9th grade or later. The earlier students opened an account, the larger the gap tended to be. The paper was published in Nature Human Behaviour.”

item.title: Young volunteers from across Europe help preserve Croatia’s traditional stone walls
item.description: Croatia Week: “Young volunteers from six European countries have arrived at Croatia’s Vransko Lake Nature Park to help protect its natural and cultural heritage through a conservation project…. Over 29 days, participants are working on several conservation activities within the nature park, including restoring traditional dry stone walls, maintaining visitor infrastructure and restoring a floodplain meadow, Vransko Lake Nature Park said.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Digital project seeks to save Cyprus’ villages from oblivion
item.description: Cyprus Mail: “In Greece, where 52-year-old [Sotiris] Makrygiannis was born (he’s half-Cypriot on his mother’s side), the situation is even worse. Of the 13,500 communities – i.e. towns and villages – in that country, 13,100 are set to become ‘ghosts’ in the next 10 years. It’s in that depressing context that Makrygiannis has launched kittim.org, a searchable database of every Cypriot village, including the occupied ones.” Available in Greek and English.

item.title: Human Rights Tribunal launches online database
item.description: The Royal Gazette (Bermuda): “The Human Rights Tribunal has launched an online database of its decisions. The website will also hold information about the tribunal and its role, functions and procedures.”

item.title: North Carolina Red Cross Chapter Highlighted in Herbert Lee Waters’ Photographs
item.description: DigitalNC: “Thanks to our partner, the Davidson County Historical Museum, we are excited to announce that a new batch of photographs by Herbert Lee Waters, better known as H. Lee Waters, is now available on DigitalNC! This latest batch contains 453 new negatives covering North Carolina life from the 1930s to the 1980s.”

item.title: I had no idea my phone could automate this much, and now it practically runs itself
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Samsung buries one of Android’s best automation tools in Settings: Modes and Routines. It handles bedtime, the car, battery, and even NFC tags. For the few things it can’t do, there’s Tasker. I started small and kept going until my phone was doing more than I could keep track of, and then I scaled it back. Here’s where that took me, plus how these ideas work on a Pixel and an iPhone.”

item.title: Greenville bridge briefly renamed on Google Maps in memory of Fiona the hippo
item.description: WYFF: “A pedestrian bridge that opened in Greenville, South Carolina, on Thursday was renamed on Google Maps in memory of Fiona, the beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo who died this week. The Verdae Pedestrian Bridge extends the Swamp Rabbit Trail’s Green Line, which supports an average of 1,000 daily users and creates a safe separation from vehicles traveling below.”

item.title: Two new tools for moving WordPress sites
item.description: Bad Sector: “Reprint and Disembark both copy a WordPress site with nothing but admin access to the source. I had Codex interrupt transfers, undo restores, and store URLs a dozen awkward ways to see what each tool gets right and what it misses.” Very extensive and thorough. Good work.

item.title: Department of Agriculture Victim of Cyberattack … Causing Concern For Country’s Food Safety
item.description: TMZ: “The U.S. Department of Agriculture was the target of a cyberattack this week … and the breach has raised serious concerns. Two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter told NBC News … the USDA told employees on Thursday that its system for paying farmers was hit.”

item.title: Google built a fake internet so Chrome’s AI doesn’t break your real one
item.description: DigitalTrends: “If you’ve watched any Doctor Strange movie, you might be familiar with the concept of the mirror world. It’s a world that reflects our own, but nothing happening there affects ours. Google is doing the same thing for testing its AI. As the company is using its Gemini models to power its AI browsing features, there was a need to take extra precautions so it doesn’t completely upend our browsing experience. ”

item.title: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember them
item.description: BBC: “On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy – a move that’s had an unexpected side effect. Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: directory of active RSS feeds
item.description: Found on Reddit: A MASSIVE (almost 35000) From the Reddit announcement: “There are 17k feeds that are active, and about 10k of them are categorized and searchable by topic. [The announcement was three days ago and the site was updated today, which I think accounts for the different numbers.] That is a fraction of the high quality feeds that are still alive on the web, and my ambition is to index hundreds of thousands of feeds. We are not there yet, but I tried to account for it in the design. It uses data from other curated lists, periodically validates feed liveness, and re-categorizes feeds into topics based on content, not just the author-assigned categories.”

item.title: Century-spanning archive of world’s oldest architectural modelmakers launches online
item.description: Arts University Bournemouth: “A major visual record of British architectural history and physical craft has been made publicly available following the launch of a new online archive dedicated to Thorp Modelmakers. Hosted at thorp.aub.ac.uk and created by Arts University Bournemouth (AUB), the digital platform preserves the extensive collection of the London-founded firm, established by John Thorp in 1883 and recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest architectural modelmaking practice in the world. Supported by a grant from the Paul Mellon Centre for Studies in British Art, the platform provides architects, researchers and historians with direct access to more than 2,500 digitised photographs of models produced between 1890 and 1995.”

item.title: WSGS launches Wyoming State Fossil Archive online catalog
item.description: County 10: “Fossils that until now were seen mostly by Wyoming State Geological Survey (WSGS) staff and academic researchers are now viewable by anyone online. The new catalog of the Wyoming State Fossil Archive at the WSGS showcases more than 150 scientifically significant fossils in the collection.”

item.title: Google Leaned Into A.I., Hurting Its Core Business
item.description: New York Times: “Over the last six months, Mr. Evans, who is based in North Carolina, has moved ad dollars away from Google search ads. For one company that sells trophies, he said, he is allocating $500 a month to the search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago, when Google introduced a feature called A.I. Mode. And he is putting more of the money toward streaming services like Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor.”

item.title: 21 Alternative Search Engines You Can Use Instead of Google
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Some give you more control over privacy and rankings, whilst others bring together sources in a conversation, search a specialist collection, or help you explore the content people use in another country. For marketers, those differences also explain why visibility beyond Google involves more than submitting a website to another engine. You don’t have to give up Google to find out what you might be missing. We collated 21 alternative search engines and tools worth trying, whether you’re looking for a better answer or a new way for customers to find your business.”

item.title: LinkedIn now lets you make your own snazzy business card. Here’s how to make one
item.description: DigitalTrends: “LinkedIn has announced a digital business card that you can share when you meet someone in person, making it easier to stay in touch. It’s customizable card that can be added to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet and shared with others through a scan. At present, it’s only available on the LinkedIn mobile app in English, and the company says it plans to make it available on more devices and languages in future.”

item.title: Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
item.description: NPR: “Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that’s built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.”

item.title: Big Tech’s compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group says
item.description: The Register: “Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry’s compliance with the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.”

item.title: Antagonistic and impulsive traits are linked to cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing on Instagram
item.description: PsyPost: “A survey of Iranian university students found that those with more pronounced Antagonism and Disinhibition, two maladaptive personality traits, were more likely to report harmful online behaviors such as cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing. In contrast, students higher in Anankastia, a trait marked by perfectionism and rigid rule-following, were less likely to report several of these behaviors. The paper was published in BMC Psychology.”

item.title: Wired Says ‘Please Let The Internet Die.’ Some Of Us Are Busy Building A Better One.
item.description: Techdirt: “It remains incredible — and disturbing — to me how many people now think of the entire internet as being made up of a few giant enshittifying companies. I understand why that is. The big companies absolutely do dominate much of the internet, and it’s close to impossible to avoid them entirely. But that doesn’t mean that that’s the entirety of the internet. And when you act as if it is, you do real damage to the good parts of the internet that still exist outside of the blast radius of those giants.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Nine Inch Nails fans can now stream nearly 2000 live recordings
item.description: CDM: “For fans of NIN and all the artists and their side projects, it’s a momentous week. For nearly 20 years, the Nine Inch Nails archive has been compiling live shows from 1988 to today; that’s now nearly 2000 recordings of over 1200 concerts. The site is a pleasure to navigate now, and this week came big news: streaming, on demand.”

item.title: Who’s behind America’s anti-trans bills? A new archive lets you follow the paper trail
item.description: The Advocate: “When a politician invokes transgender people in a campaign ad, sponsors a bill restricting their rights or votes to pass it, that history can be remarkably hard to piece together. The ad lives in one archive, the bill on a state website, the hearing in hours of committee video. If someone sues, the next chapter unfolds on a court docket. The Trans Data Initiative, announced November 9, brings those records together in a free national archive.”

item.title: Before You Sign That Lease: A New Website Ranks D.C.’s “Worst Landlords”
item.description: Washington City Paper: “The website uses public data to map open housing violations and highlight the District’s most egregious repeat offenders…. Stomp Out Slumlords’ watch list also goes beyond the LLCs that own the buildings, which often obscure the identities of the people behind them. According to the group’s press release, organizers cross-referenced corporate filings to trace corporate ownership structures directly to the individuals at the top.”

item.title: YouTube Reportedly Nearing Multi-Billion Settlement With School Districts Over Social Media Addiction, Harms
item.description: Gizmodo: “Google subsidiary YouTube is finalizing a settlement with school districts that have sued it over claims that the streaming giant deliberately designed YouTube to be addictive with no regard for mental health, Bloomberg reported on Friday.”

item.title: This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping
item.description: PetaPixel: “A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo. HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.”

item.title: Tech Outages May Become Routine. Experts Say Don’t Panic, but Prepare.
item.description: New York Times: “… with A.I. exposing vulnerabilities in our software and companies rushing to fix them, experts say disruptions could last several more months or longer — and the next one could test our dependence on digital services like phone-based payment systems or online banking. Here are some practical steps people can take to prepare.”

item.title: Outage at NSA’s highly classified communications network has been resolved, sources say
item.description: CNN: “The outage of a key internal communications network at the National Security Agency that has kept large swaths of employees locked out for more than three days has now been resolved, according to a source familiar with the matter and a voicemail inbox recording for employees at the main headquarters in Maryland.”

item.title: TikTok launches tool to help public figures detect deepfakes globally
item.description: AFP: “TikTok announced Friday the global launch of its deepfake-detection tool for public figures as the social media platform seeks to curb AI-generated disinformation ahead of a wave of European elections next year.”

item.title: GTA VI didn’t break the internet, thanks to ‘stupid DNS tricks’
item.description: The Register: “Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th. Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.”

item.title: Syrian photographer reunites with memories hidden behind wall for over a decade
item.description: Anadolu Ajansı: “A Syrian photographer has recovered his personal archive after more than a decade, tearing down a wall he built to conceal the entrance to his library in the northern city of Raqqa before fleeing the country’s war. Ahmed al-Bekkar, 66, who sought refuge in Türkiye amid destruction, looting and attacks by the Daesh (ISIS) terrorist group and forces of Syria’s now-ousted regime, had sealed off his library to protect his books, photographs and personal documents.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: 50 Years of Vision: How Alice O’Leary Randall Became the Keeper of the Medical Cannabis Story
item.description: Cannabis Media Council: “In 1976, a Washington D.C., court acquitted Robert Randall of marijuana possession on the grounds of medical necessity. He and Alice spent the next 20 years fighting to make that access available to other patients. After Robert died in 2001, Alice became the keeper of the story, and now — 50 years after the historical court decision — she’s sharing her story with us. Read her legal saga and love story below and dive even deeper by visiting our Cannabis Media Council’s 50 Years of Vision destination.”

item.title: New website celebrates a century of greyhound racing in Britain
item.description: Greyhound Board of Great Britain: “As the sport’s centenary year draws to a close, the 100 Years on Track website has been created by the Greyhound Board of Great Britain (GBGB) as a lasting legacy of the celebrations. Serving as a new digital home for greyhound racing’s rich heritage and memorabilia, the website launches with a collection of historic photographs, artefacts and personal stories from across the decades. As further contributions are made by owners, trainers and racing enthusiasts, it will continue to evolve into a comprehensive archive of the sport’s history.”

item.title: 27,000 reasons not to download “GTA VI for PC”
item.description: DigitalTrends: “You can’t be on the internet and not feel like you’re missing out on the GTA VI hype train if you’re a PC gamer. But before you get desperate and go digging for a ‘totally legit’ copy of the game for PC, you might want to read this. Kaspersky has recorded 27,416 detections of GTA VI-related malware and unwanted apps since June and is warning PC players out there looking for a version of the game that doesn’t exist.”

item.title: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “WordPress 7.2 is due on Dec. 8. This version has, in beta, turned on a new public address on updated sites. /random/ directs you to a random published post. Versions of the address also do this within categories, tags, author archives, or eligible custom post types.”

item.title: More young hikers lost using Google Maps on Lake District fells, say rescuers
item.description: BBC: “More young people are getting caught out on the fells due to relying on Google Maps for navigation, rescuers have said. After a full-team rescue on Sunday, Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team (WMRT) said an increasing amount of young people, mostly aged 18 to 24, were getting lost or into trouble after using Google Maps on their phones.”

item.title: The Internet Archive’s workers are unionizing
item.description: Engadget: “Workers at the Internet Archive, home to the Wayback Machine, are unionizing. After signing up to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA), they’re asking founder Brewster Kahle to voluntarily recognize the union. As a backup, they’ve filed for a National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) election. Kahle hasn’t responded publicly yet.”

item.title: The FBI was hacked again, this time the breach targeted its crime database
item.description: CNN: “The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement, two people briefed on the investigation said. The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers is the second such breach in recent months.”

item.title: New US Bill Seeks To Track Russian Hybrid Attacks
item.description: Radio Free Europe: “Three Democratic lawmakers have proposed new legislation that would require the State Department to regularly report to Congress on hybrid or shadow-warfare activities attributed to Russia. The proposed legislation, known as the Warning Allies and Tracking Covert Hostilities by Russia (WATCH Russia) Act, comes amid growing concern about sabotage, cyberattacks, and other covert operations in Europe.”

item.title: Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again
item.description: ZDNet: “Privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set new limits on screenshots. The company will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and ‘when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,’ Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday. Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.”

item.title: Feed algorithms shape the misinformation supply, not only what users believe
item.description: Harvard Kennedy Schools Misinformation Review: “Debates about platform effects keep asking whether ranked feeds change an individual’s beliefs. That question matters, but it misses a second effect. Ranking systems reward some messages, teach the people who post what travels, and gradually change the supply of information available to everyone. Treating engagement ranking as a selection environment clarifies why mixed findings about short-term persuasion can coexist with serious ecosystem risks. It also points toward better research, audits, and platform design.”

item.title: American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it
item.description: ScienceNews: “… at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, [Rebecca] Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer ‘fit the Agency’s current needs.’ In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.”

item.title: Dental students put Medicaid data on the map
item.description: Harvard Gazette: “In February 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services released a massive Medicaid claims dataset spanning 2018 to 2024, opening millions of anonymized records to the public. While the agency touted the data as a way to expose fraud, three third-year Harvard School of Dental Medicine students saw another possibility: using dental claims to reveal gaps in care and help researchers explore differences in oral health access across the U.S.” Good morning, Internet…
